articles.title: Closing the Afghan file
articles.content: THE civil-military relationship in Pakistan has never been ideal. Despite recent conciliatory efforts and the policy of accommodation adopted by the coalition government, concerns within security-focused circles persist about the handling of several government affairs. For now, though, there is little chance of an escalation in civil-military tensions involving the federal and provincial governments; the last hitch was the PTI government, which was ousted throughgovernor’s rule and emergency. The major allegation against the PTI government has been that it was hesitant to take a clear position against the terrorists, enabling them to expand their influence in parts of the province, especially in the southern districts. The establishment is sensitive about the narrative, and considers it subversion and part of hybrid warfare; it looks upon any political or ideological support for it as support to the enemy. Terminology describing Taliban-aligned terrorists as ‘Fitna al-Khwarij’ and Baloch insurgents as ‘Fitna al-Hindustan’ reflects the same approach. Everyone is expected to follow this approach; the PTI government’s disagreement on several security-related policies is, therefore, interpreted as an act of subversion. Meanwhile, it is clear how much civilian governments actually contribute to security-related affairs. The security domain has often caused friction between the establishment and civilian governments; over the decades, the political leadership has learned not to voice disagreement on security-related affairs. ‘Memogate’ was the last such lesson for the PPP; and ‘Dawnleaks’ for Mian Nawaz Sharif; the removal of Imran Khan’s PTI from its provincial seat of power in KP appears to have followed the same pattern. The story is not simply about subversion or disagreement over security policy. There are other relevant aspects that some commentators have pointed out: among them is the fiscal issue which also triggered the call for new provinces and the reversal of the 18th Amendment. Yet another dimension is linked to closing the Afghan file. Bhutto’s policy was just the lever. It was Zia who turned it into an ideology. The Afghan policy has shaped Pakistan’s politics for half a century; but now there is a general acceptance, even within security circles, that it has not worked. It is evident that the state is distancing itself from past approaches. In this regard, some intellectuals and commentators have painted militancy as a cultural expression of Pakhtuns, which the local dynamics of the larger Pakhtun society has aggravated. There is no need to deconstruct such a perception, which would be stigmatisation. In effect, applying a sociocultural lens to the issue takes away focus from the main architects of the security and Afghan policy. The previous Afghan policy worked well but had lost its utility in geopolitical contexts. This was the policy crafted by the military dictator Gen Ziaul Haq and his team, and it was more or less functional until the Taliban captured power in Afghanistan in August 2021. Though the Zia file saw a few changes and amendments, the overall framework for dealing with these affairs did not change much. The Zia file had a few critical components that even allies including Washington, Beijing, Riyadh, and Ankara had concerns about — particularly the reliance on non-state actors. Mian Nawaz Sharif had drawn attention to it but faced the consequences. Many analysts believe that this flawed policy was responsible for spawning the TTP and generating terrorism in KP but official narratives do not link the state of affairs to the policy choices made earlier. Establishment circles appear to want a new Afghan policy that best suits their geopolitical and internal security objectives. A complete detachment from the Taliban is part of the new approach, and the Sohail Afridi government was reluctant to adopt it because it would mean a large-scale military operation, displacement, and increased security-related resource allocation — which would also have political consequences. After the removal of his government, the hurdles preventing a new policy have been eliminated; the new set-up now has to deliver, as was expected of the Afridi government. There will be no opportunity any longer to shift the onus of blame onto a political government, despite official narratives distancing the security state from political change in KP. However, the dimensions of the new Afghan policy remain unclear. For instance, how will the state proceed if the Afghan Taliban agree to detach themselves from the terrorist networks operating against Pakistan from Afghan soil? Still, another argument being promoted is that Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, not Gen Ziaul Haq, was the real architect of Pakistan’s Afghan policy. There is some truth to that. After Sardar Daud’s 1973 coup in Kabul and his revival of the Pakhtunistan issue, the Bhutto government began hosting and training Afghan Islamists, among them men who would later become the commanders of the anti-Soviet jihad. The FC and a small circle of officials ran this as a pressure tool against Kabul. Notably, the province’s first governor after 1973, appointed in 1975, following the ban on the National Awami Party, reflected the same anxieties about Pakhtun nationalism and Afghanistan. But Bhutto’s policy was just the lever. It was Zia who turned it into an ideology. After the Soviet invasion of 1979, the Afghan question became the organising principle of the state: the jihad, the refugee economy, the madressah network, the doctrine of strategic depth, and an intelligence apparatus that grew more powerful than the elected institutions meant to oversee it. That legacy matters, and it is Zia’s. Now it is up to the supporters of the PPP how they take the argument, and whether they are ready to carry the entire burden of history on their shoulders; they also face criticism that Benazir Bhutto continued Bhutto’s legacy and allowed Gen Naseerullah Babar to nurture the Taliban in 1994-96, the same general who had crafted the Afghan files for her father. The Taliban generations have caused huge losses to the PPP, including the assassination of Benazir Bhutto herself.
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: Safe spaces for women
articles.content: THE Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010, was an important response to problems that directly affect women. It enabled the ombudsman to hear cases, many of which were resolved in women’s favour. A recent judgement has now eliminated an avenue that many women used to report harassment. The Federal Constitutional Court’sruling, which narrows the interpretation of harassment, is a setback for women’s space in public life. Unfortunately, it appears to show that a major state institution is prepared to restrict rather than expand women’s safety at work. From birth to death, women and girls in Pakistan face limits on where they can go freely, where they may go only under certain conditions, and where they cannot go at all. Visitors to Pakistan often notice their limited visibility as one of the first features of public life. This absence should not be dismissed as cultural; it largely reflects structural factors. Restrictions on mobility — driven mainly by concerns about safety — help explain poor educational outcomes for girls, physical inactivity during adolescence, and their alarmingly low participation in the labour force as adults. The lack of safety outside the home is among the most frequently cited reasons for not sending girls to school, alongside poverty and families’ inability to afford schooling. The problem is intensified by the limited availability of girls’ schools in many parts of Pakistan. Undoubtedly, the shortage of schools and female teachers, together with poor learning quality, creates major barriers. Millions of girls live in districts where the nearest public school is more than an hour away and therefore out of practical reach. These supply-side failures prevent many girls from even imagining that they could enter a classroom. Perceived danger reinforces the barrier at home: some girls never enrol, while others drop out at puberty. At the very least, girls who are fortunate enough to live near a school should not be excluded because the journey is unsafe. Women’s limited ability to work outside the home is probably the most affected by structural factors. A Population Council and Unicef study,Adolescent Girls’ Voices on Enhancing Their Own Productivity, found that parents were reluctant to send girls to school because of fear of harassment on the way. This fear has been exacerbated by an incredible surge in social media-related harassment and cyberbullying, thanks to the proliferation of mobile phones and other digital devices. Requiring a chaperone or private transport immediately increases the costs of sending girls to school. Not surprisingly, an estimated 8.3 million girls aged 10 to 19 lack official status — they are neither in school, at work, nor married. This large cohort of girls depicts a decade of lost productivity, learning, and, above all, self-esteem. The state’s role is clear: protect the rights of all its citizens from harassment and unsafe spaces. It must remove these hurdles by providing structural solutions that enable girls to attend and complete school. Harassment laws that create safe routes and workplaces must be seen as educational policy requirements, not peripheral issues. Women’s limited ability to work outside the home is probably the most affected by structural factors. It is also the most costly in terms of losses to the economy and society. Female labour force participation rates have remained stagnant at around 22 per cent for the last 15 years. When women earn, they tend to spend more proactively, with direct payoffs for children’s education, health, and general welfare. But this will not happen if women feel unprotected at the workplace. Although women are generally accepted as schoolteachers and in some health professions, attacks on doctors and Lady Health Workers threaten even these spaces — many work mostly out of economic desperation. Employers are reluctant to give women jobs with longer, more secure contracts because of perceived hazards and domestic duties. At the other end of the spectrum, highly educated and affluent women participate in the labour force, cushioned by family support and private transport. The result is some improvement in women’s participation at the top end for highly educated, privileged women and, at the other end, for the truly desperate who must leave home to buy food and ensure their families’ survival, ie, domestic help, cleaners, and informal sector workers who do the most menial work. Women’s representation in Pakistan’s parliament is the only positive achievement in the SDGs’ gender indicators. Most elected women come from privileged families, but not all, as the pool expands. The trend began with the mandatory party quota for women. Otherwise, trends of an even more male-dominated parliament would have continued. The handful of women lawmakers have made headway in legislating, or at least highlighting, issues important to women and human rights. Comparable action is required in laws and public policy to expand women’s participation in every public sphere, especially formal employment. Increasing the number of women in decision-making and other critical positions — particularly in the police and judiciary — would make a tangible difference. A 30pc recruitment quota in the formal sector is essential. Greater representation in formal paid work will generate positive spillover effects in other sectors. It is especially imperative to address the extremely high unemployment rate (24pc) among young women who have completed more than a secondary education. Despite completing higher levels of education, this group is denied opportunities for secure employment. A quota system and positive supportive legislation will directly and positively affect the current generation whom we repeatedly say we care about the most. Women and girls must have safe passage and be guarded with assurances that harassment is a punishable offence. Recent measures to improve women’s mobility are encouraging, such as pink buses and scooter loans, but they remain too few and too far apart. Above all, there is a need to change mindsets; a public campaign against harassment of women and girls in public spaces must become a priority. Society must review its standards and morals and move forward, not backwards, in legislation, run bold campaigns, and do whatever it takes to correct this pernicious course of restricting, rather than expanding, the power of women and girls. The writer is country adviser to the Population Council.
articles.author: Zeba Sathar

articles.title: Moral consensus
articles.content: CANADA’S richest province Ontario, with a GDP of a trillion Canadian dollars, purchased a 10-year-old jet costing 28 million Canadian dollars (Rs5.46 billion) for the official use of its premier. Critics quickly dubbed it the “gravy plane”, taunting Doug Ford’s long-standing political rhetoric about eliminating government waste. The premier was quick to take responsibility. He promptly returned the plane. Far away, in a country where 48 per cent of the people fall in the ‘extremely poor’ category, a chief minister acquired a spanking new Gulfstream 500 — twice as expensive as the plane of the Ontarian premier. It was also followed by similar public outrage. The chief minister, however, vowed to continue using the “gravy plane” as her legal right. On Sept 30, 2026, something seriously went wrong with the execution of Christa Pike at the Maximum Security Prison in Nashville, Tennessee. The two doses of the lethal pentobarbital injection failed to achieve their intended result. Pike did not die. Just two days later, Frank Strada, commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Correction, resigned on grounds of moral responsibility. Only a few weeks earlier, 14 newborn babies had been burnt to death in a hospital fire in Islamabad. No one resigned. The executive director had to be forced to step down. Why is it that countries possessing very similar constitutions, parliaments, democracies, and laws end up achieving radically different outcomes? The ones doing poorly can be recognised by a distinct common denominator: a ruling class deeply deficient in character, values, and moral responsibility. Such nations forever remain in search of new laws, new faces, and new messiahs, rather than seeking a new code of conduct for their morally deficient leaders. Laws devoid of morality find enough loopholes to justify abuse. For centuries, slavery was legally permitted. Women were legally denied their right to vote and property. Racial segregation and discrimination were once legally enforced. Children working long hours in hazardous jobs was legally permitted. Workers dying or being seriously injured in mines and sewage gutters was treated as the cost of doing business. But all these ‘legally’ sanctioned practices were inherently unjust and morally decadent. It took decades of determined struggle by the abolitionist, women’s rights, civil rights, and labour movements to establish that legality alone could never legitimise practices that violated the fundamental principles of equality, dignity, safety, and justice. While Pakistani laws adequately address equality, safety, and dignity, the ruling elite has remained resolutely impervious to any of these considerations and continues to rule with remarkable immorality. Governance has become synonymous with self-enrichment, self-projection, and self-indulgence. Questioning the conduct, wastefulness and misuse of state resources is considered unpatriotic. Pakistan thus faces a grave moral and institutional crisis that cannot be resolved by any new sermons, slogans, changes in government, or enactment of new laws. An ecosystem overflowing with laws but devoid of morality will always find enough loopholes and justifications to perpetuate its questionable practices. Much as the abolition of slavery required society to move beyond what the law permitted, Pakistan needs a moral consensus on rejecting practices that may be legally permissible yet remain immoral, unequal, undignified, unsafe, and irresponsible. A useful starting point would be to recognise that expenditures such as aircraft and bullet-proof vehicles for the luxury and convenience of the ruling elite, even when legally sanctioned, are downright immoral, and should be withdrawn. The excessive self-sanctioned salaries, perks and privileges of judges, parliamentarians, and government officials, even when backed by legal notifications, are im- moral. Billions of rupees spent on self-publicity, ads, billboards, posters and pictures on every imaginable free space, even when approved by a sycophantic finance department, are wasteful and unethical. Likewise, naming every building, bridge, school, hospital, and ration bag after a serving politician is morally reprehensible. Sending workers into sewage gutters, even when legally practised for 80 years is despicably immoral and needs to be eliminated forthwith. Not to mention that pathological addiction of borrowing and begging from foreign donors and friendly countries, even when endorsed by law, is demeaning and immoral. Pakistan must pause, introspect and agree on how to weed out immorality amongst leaders. An agenda for moral reforms that binds the rulers to higher standards of conduct may be far more consequential than a new or recycled set of laws and leaders. The writer is an industrial engineer and a volunteer social activist.
articles.author: Naeem Sadiq

articles.title: ‘The joke is on us’
articles.content: THE post began with an apology. The writer Amitava Kumar explained that Facebook had blocked his Substack link in India, so he was sharing his essay as plain text instead. I read that line twice. Then I laughed, because I recognised it. In Pakistan, we know this routine well. The link that won’t open. The site that loads everywhere except here. The workaround that everyone shares and no one in authority admits is needed. Kumar was writing about the young Indians who call themselves cockroaches. Their movement began as satire, a joke party mocking the government over a leaked medical entrance exam. Then it became the Cockroach Janta Party. For over a month, young people camped at Jantar Mantar – Delhi’s iconic protest site. Now their anger has turned on a revision of the voter rolls that has, reportedly, stripped millions of their right to vote. Last week, the state responded with brute force: thousands of protesters and journalists were detained; CJP leaders were picked up on arrival in Delhi, and mobile and internet services were jammed in most parts of the capital. India’s mainstream television channels looked the other way. Seen from here, none of this looks new. We have lived through nationwide internet suspensions. We spent more than a year with X blocked. We have watched names vanish from television screens, speeches go unaired, and protests barricaded before they began. We have seen leaders detained on their way to rallies and journalists told, politely or otherwise, what not to cover. If the government across the border has a playbook, some of its chapters were written here. But the cockroaches have a playbook too, and it is one we also know. They named themselves after the creature everyone wants to crush but can never eradicate. It is a brilliant choice. An insult became a badge. A threat became a punchline. Their posters are irreverent, often profane and frequently very funny, in a culture where young people are raised to be respectful towards their elders. Reporters at the protests have described crowds fanning each other in the heat, laughing into the police’s eyeglasses with facial recognition. Humour is what people use when the usual channels close. Humour is what people use when the usual channels close. It is harder to arrest and cheaper than a lawyer. Pakistanis understand this instinctively. Under Ziaul Haq, satire went underground and survived. In recent years, when television fell silent on certain subjects, the jokes simply moved online. A meme can say what a news anchor cannot, and a whole generation has learned to read between the punchlines. When the media looks away, someone else fills the gap. In India, young reporters and small digital outlets have covered the protests that big channels ignored. One protest site even had a wall honouring the journalists who showed up. That, too, is familiar. In Pakistan, some of the most important reporting of the past few years has come from people working with a phone, a YouTube channel — and very little protection. Kumar wrote in the same post about another writer urging his fellow guests to “celebrate the cockroach”. Young Indians, he said, had given the country its most hopeful moment in a long time. The sentiment is understandable. There is something moving about young people who refuse to be solemn, who meet barricades with jokes and detentions with more jokes. But hope is not the same as change, and the state has a long memory and a large budget. Laughter can sustain a movement. It cannot, on its own, win one. It is tempting, from this side of the border, to watch India’s troubles with a certain satisfaction. I would resist that. The tools being used against India’s young protesters are not foreign to us. Neither is the courage of those using humour to fight back. What is happening in Delhi is less a story about India than a story about the region, about governments that have learned to switch off the internet faster than they can create jobs, and young people who have learned to make jokes faster than governments can ban them. There is one difference, and it is worth naming. India has long called itself the world’s largest democracy. That claim is what makes the barricades at Jantar Mantar so jarring to watch. We have never made such grand claims about ourselves. Perhaps that is honesty. Perhaps it is simply lowered expectations. Either way, when I look at Delhi and see a reflection of the state of affairs at home, I am not sure who should be more embarrassed. The cockroaches are laughing. The state is cutting the internet. And from across the border, it all looks very familiar. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: State of denial
articles.content: AS reports continue to do the rounds of possible Russian mediation to resolve the differences between Pakistan and Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, the Foreign Office hasunderscoredthat successful dialogue requires commitment from Kabul to end cross-border terrorism. This demand is neither new nor unreasonable; it highlights the point that talks and support for anti-Pakistan terrorist groups cannot go hand in hand. On Friday, the FO said that while it was not aware of any formal Russian mediation initiative, Pakistan was open to engagement that produced tangible results. Representatives of Pakistan and the Taliban regime were both in Russia earlier this month as part of the Moscow Format regionalconsultations.A joint communique could not be issued at the conclave due to frosty Islamabad-Kabul ties, specifically because the Taliban objected to including any references to terrorism in Afghanistan. Russia had offered its good offices to resolve the impasse, if both sides required its help. The official Taliban position amounts to a state of denial: it is hardly a secret that some of the world’s most dangerous terrorist groups find shelter in Afghanistan. Therefore, the Kabul regime’s denials hold no water. Many other third parties — Qatar, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and China — have tried to mediate between Pakistan and Afghanistan, with varying degrees of success. Russia is the only state thatrecognises the Taliban regime. Perhaps Moscow can be engaged by Pakistan and Afghanistan to try and give the peace process another chance. Pakistan and Afghanistan share borders and linguistic and cultural links. Good relations are essential, even though bilateral relations have remained largely strained over the past several decades. However, the biggest obstacle to long-term peace is the Taliban’s sheltering of terrorist groups. Pakistan desires peace, but for talks to succeed, Kabul must offer visible CBMs, such as an end to cross-border terrorism. As the FO has said, a “verifiable mechanism” that ensures an end to anti-Pakistan terrorism emanating from Afghanistan can lead the way to peace. Kabul’s claims that it is not hosting violent groups are of little value. Action against such groups is required, not hollow refutations. Moreover, regional states must realise that today it is Pakistan that is battling terrorist groups in Afghanistan. Tomorrow, similar violent actors based in that country can destabilise other regional states. Russia itself has been targeted by IS-K terrorism. The group finds a home in Afghanistan, even though it is at daggers drawn with the Taliban. If the Taliban regime commits to preventing groups based on its soil from attacking neighbouring states, the process of normalisation and regional integration of Afghanistan can begin.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Suffering in silence
articles.content: TOO many Pakistani children have nowhere to turn when abused online. An estimated 1.5m internet-using children aged 12 to 17 experienced sexual exploitation or abuse involving digital technology in the year preceding a nationwide survey conducted in 2025. This is cited in the Disrupting Harm in Pakistan report, produced by Unicef, ECPAT International, and Interpol. As disturbing as the scale is, what happened afterwards is equally alarming. More than half the affected children told nobody, while none of those surveyed who experienced abuse approached formal reporting channels. In 85pc of incidents, the offender was someone the children knew. Social media accounted for 44pc of reported incidents. These findings expose a serious weakness in Pakistan’s child-protection system: children are suffering abuse, often at the hands of people they know, without being able to seek help. Fear of blame, humiliation, and punishment at home can be enough to silence them. Some worry that their families will restrict their access to phones or the internet instead of confronting the abuser. Boys face additional barriers because sexual abuse against them is rarely discussed openly. Behind these figures are children who may continue to suffer threats and blackmail because they see no safe way out. The government’s responsibility cannot end with passing laws against online exploitation. Those laws mean little to a child who does not know where to report abuse or fears what might happen afterwards. Pakistan needs reporting services that children can reach easily and use confidentially, with trained staff who know how to respond without judgement. Schools should help children recognise abuse and understand where to seek help, while parents must respond with reassurance rather than scepticism or punishment. Equally important is what happens once a complaint is made. The study identifies gaps in legal protections for children during investigations, including the absence of a requirement that forensic interviews be conducted by specially trained professionals. This must change. Children should not have to recount traumatic experiences repeatedly or face questioning that leaves them feeling responsible for what happened. The National Commission on the Rights of Child has called for stronger cybercrime investigation capabilities and specialised units. These proposals deserve attention, resources and oversight.
articles.author: Editorial
